newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Israel must backtrack in Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Israel must backtrack in Jerusalem.

text.p: Egypt said on Wednesday an Israeli retreat from its decision to build a settlement in Jerusalem must be the starting-point for resuming Middle East peace talks.
Israeli leaders said on Wednesday that work on the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim would continue and that peace talks could resume only when Palestinian violence stopped.
But in Cairo, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa set out the incompatible Arab position.

"To save the peace process needs political statesmanship and courage. The practices and steps that have been taken in Jerusalem will have to be rolled back. This is the starting-point for any effort to save the process," he said.

"We count on Europe and all of those forces including Europe, insisting on the continuation of the American role based on the notion of honest broker and a balanced approach," Moussa added, hinting at Arab doubts about Washington's neutrality.
Moussa was speaking after talks on the Middle East crisis with Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who is on a regional tour as president of the European Union council.
Van Mierlo said again that he had doubts about an Arab League decision to step back from normal relations with Israel and reinstate the economic boycott.

Arab foreign ministers took the decision on Monday in response to the Jabal Abu Ghneim settlement, which has convinced Arabs that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is using the peace process to grab more land for Israel.

"I understand very well the resolution of the Arab League as an expression of regret and protest, that I understand, but I just have my doubts whether the phrasing and the boycott are the right methods," van Mierlo said.

Moussa and the Dutch minister also discussed preparations for the European-Mediterranean conference taking place in Malta later this month and Egypt's negotiations with the European Union on an association agreement on trade.
"There are very positive signs that the conference in Malta has all the possibility to become a success," van Mierlo said.
